blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Ottoman Divan poetry is composed in aruz, a quantitative meter based on the weights of syllables. The meter is sensitive to specific characters recorded in the original writing in the Arabic script. This work is concerned with automatic meter finding and scansion alignment for Ottoman Divan poetry, especially on modern Turkish spelling without the special diacritics that scholarly transliterations of Ottoman preserve. We define two tasks on this input, first identifying the meter used in the poem, and second aligning the meter's weights with the syllabification of the poem, identifying the flaws and freedoms the poet has taken along the way. We build a corpus of 52,000 lines split by poet, with scansion annotations for 500 test lines, and a robustness benchmark generated at the deviation rates measured on real web and OCR copies. Our model is a hidden Markov model over the positions of each meter, decoded over a lattice of every candidate path, and trained by EM from the printed meter, without scansion labels. On a held-out set it scans 77.6% of the test lines fully correctly, against 26.8% for the available rule-based scanner, 55.0% for a neural tagger trained with the same supervision and 63.6% for Claude Opus 5.5 few-shot. The code is open-sourced and the tool is released on the web.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Scansion, the task of assigning a rhythmic structure to a written line of
poetry, is a sequence labeling problem that NLP has approached with rules,
HMMs, CRFs, neural taggers and LLMs ( Agirrezabal et al., 2016 ; Agirrezabal et al., 2017 ; Ruiz Fabo et al., 2026 ) . One type of verse
that has received relatively little attention in this context is Ottoman Divan poetry, the
classical Turkish poetry of the educated elite, written from the
late thirteenth century to the second half of the nineteenth century. Divan poetry is composed in a
quantitative meter called aruz , taken over from
Arabic and Persian poetry ( Çetin, 1991 ; İpekten, 2010 ) . In aruz every
syllable is either open or closed, closed if its vowel is long or it ends
in a consonant, open otherwise. Each meter fixes a sequence of short and
long positions, and a line fills it with open and closed syllables. In this paper, we address
the scansion of Divan poetry: identifying a poem’s meter and aligning each
syllable of each line to its position in that meter.

blocks.en:
An automated tool that can robustly determine a Divan poem’s meter and align
each syllable has many uses for Turkish literature researchers and
poetry readers. The meter directly influences prosody, since a reader who is not aware of the correct meter cannot recite the line correctly. Finding it by hand is slow and
error-prone even for trained readers, who can disagree on the same
poem ( Kurt and Kara, 2012 ) , and it is a standing difficulty for students of
Turkish literature. Editors depend on the scansion, since a line that will not scan is the sign of a
misreading or a misprint ( Köksal, 2009 ) . And more than a thousand divan collections remain in
Turkish libraries, many of them unstudied ( Kurt and Kara, 2012 ) . Tracing the meters, flaws
and choices of poets across eras would benefit greatly from an automated
scanner.

The problem is not trivial, for two main reasons. The first is the script. The
poems were written in the Arabic alphabet, which records the long vowels and
consonants the meter counts. Since the alphabet reform of 1928 ( Lewis, 1999 ) ,
Turkish has been written in Latin letters, and the original texts, in a script few now
read and hard to OCR, remain largely
without machine-readable text ( Kirmizialtin and Wrisley, 2022 ) . Scholarly
editions mark modern Latin with diacritics to signify differences in the original writing, but most readers use this
poetry in plain modern Turkish spelling, in school, on websites or
typed from a manuscript, without special diacritics
(§ 2 ). A scanner must therefore work from modern spelling, where
the weights have to be restored, and should not depend on the scholarly marks
even when they are present, since editions do not always supply them and can be incorrect or inconsistent. Here is

The second reason is that, even when the original letters are known, a line does not always
match its meter syllable for syllable. Aruz tolerates a set of departures from
the expected weights, called flaws
( kusur ) ( Düzenli and Bulak, 2018 ) . For example an open syllable may fill a long
position, a closed one a short position, and a word may or may not be linked
to the next (§ 2 ). In the couplet above, the open second syllable
of dahi fills a long position and is read with a long vowel. These are not marked in the text, and which flaws a line takes is
determined by the meter of the poem, not by the line itself, so a single line
admits many readings.

These decisions cannot be made syllable by syllable. Whether a syllable takes
a flaw depends on the syllables before and after it, and on the meter, which
is not given. Since a single line often fits more than one meter, the meter,
and with it the reading of every line, can only be settled for the poem as a
whole.

blocks.en:
Computational work on aruz has concentrated on Arabic
(§ 8 ). Rule-based systems ( Abuata and Al-Omari, 2018 ) and recurrent
networks ( Yousef et al., 2019 ; Al-shaibani et al., 2020 ) identify the meter of
a verse and they work on Arabic script. For Ottoman poetry the only system we know
of is that of Kurt and Kara (2012) , which is a deterministic rule-based algorithm running on scholarly edition strings. It is bound by the scholarly
transliteration. It reads the syllable weights directly off the edition’s
letters, so it cannot be used on the modern spelling, and
even on scholarly text a long-vowel mark the edition left out
is recognized as a flaw instead of being corrected. This over-dependence on the scholarly edition input makes the system prone to mistakes. Large language models, used zero- or few-shot, are the obvious
alternative. As we show in § 7 , the strongest models we tried,
prompted with the rules, the meters and worked examples, read at best
63.6% of held-out lines correctly.

We first define two tasks on a poem given in plain modern Turkish spelling
with no meter marked, a form to which a scholarly transcription reduces by
removing its diacritics, identifying the poem’s meter, and scanning each of
its lines with every syllable’s position in the meter and any flaw it takes.
For these tasks we build a corpus of 52,000 lines from thirteen critical
editions, split by poet, and scansion annotations for 500 test lines
(§ 3 , § 4 ).

Our model follows from the difficulties above. A trained spelling model proposes
scholarly forms for each word, and every reading of the line these forms allow
is laid out in a lattice. A hidden Markov model over the positions of the meters
scores the paths through that lattice. The only supervision is
the printed meter of each training poem, from which the model is trained by EM
(§ 5 ). We compare it with the scanner of Kurt and Kara (2012) run on
the same spelling model, a neural tagger trained with the same
supervision, and with two large language models, and we examine which parts of the model
account for the difference (§ 6 , § 7 ).
Since the text people actually scan is rarely clean edition text, we also
build a perturbation benchmark at the deviation rates measured on web and OCR
copies and test every system but the language models on it (§ 4 , § 7 ). The code and data pipeline are released at https://github.com/MehmetETiryaki/aruz-paper , and the model is freely available as a web tool at https://mehmetemretiryaki.com/aruz .

blocks.en: 2 Aruz
blocks.zh: 2 阿鲁兹

blocks.en:
Aruz counts syllables by weight, not by stress. A syllable is open if
it ends in a short vowel, as ka , and closed if it ends in a long
vowel or a consonant, as kā or kal . Some syllables, those with a
long vowel followed by a consonant, as kār , or a short vowel followed by
two consonants, as kalb , hold the place of a closed syllable followed by
an open one; these are overlong syllables ( medli ), and the reading is called medd . The last syllable of a line counts as closed regardless
of its letters ( İpekten, 2010 ) .

The Arabic alphabet writes the long vowels and the consonants, so the weight
of a syllable can be read from the original once the word is known ( Buğday, 2009 ) . Scholarly editions keep this
in their transcription, with a macron on long vowels ( ā , ī , ū ) and the signs ʿ and ʾ for ayn and hemze , two
consonants Turkish does not pronounce but the meter counts. The modern
spelling has neither, and marks a long vowel with a circumflex only where the
word would otherwise be confused with another ( Lewis, 1999 ; Yeşilöz, 2021 ) .

mnemonic word whose own syllables have the foot’s

Poets often depart from the rules above to fit the words and meaning they
want into the meter. A flaw ( kusur ) is a reading in which a syllable
does not fill the slot that proper application of the rules requires. Four main flaws are discussed. In imâle , the most common flaw, an open syllable fills a long position and

blocks.en:
The lattice holds every reading of a line. What remains is to decide which
reading is right and under which meter. We do this with a hidden Markov
model whose hidden states are the positions of a meter and whose observed
symbols are the labels of a reading. The first foot of the poem’s meter in
Figure 2 , for instance, is the four positions x, ∪ \scriptstyle\cup , – , – , and the reading kāmˑ gī‿rü is explained by these four positions
emitting, in order, the labels 𝖫 \mathsf{L} , 𝖧 \mathsf{H} , 𝖫 \mathsf{L} and 𝖲 \mathsf{S} . For each of the
seventeen templates (Appendix A ) the model has a left-to-right
chain of match states, one per position, of kind long, short or free
(the last position of a line, and the first where the meter allows either, x). A path through a chain is one line of that
template. After each match state there is an insert state, which takes
one extra syllable the template has no place for, and over each match state
there is a skip, which passes over one missing position. Neither can be
repeated in a row. Inserts and skips account for lines the meter does not,
such as a misprint in an edition or an error in a copy. The chains are joined
only at bos and eos , so a path stays within one template. A long
position emits 𝖫 \mathsf{L} most of the time and a short one 𝖲 \mathsf{S} . The probability
of emitting any other label, which is what a flaw is, is learned from data
and shared by all chains (Figure 3 ). In the example, the long
fourth position emits 𝖲 \mathsf{S} for rü , an imâle. The match, insert and skip
layout is that of a profile HMM ( Krogh et al., 1994 ) , with emissions
shared across positions of the same kind instead of learned per position.
The probability of a reading under a meter is the probability that the
positions of one of the meter’s templates, taken in order, emit the labels of
that reading. Laid against the lattice, the model is a trellis whose rows are
the positions and whose columns are the nodes of the lattice, and a path
through the trellis is one reading placed on the positions
(Figure 4 ).

blocks.en:
Training uses only the printed meter of each poem. A training line is built
into a lattice as above, but from the edition’s own spelling, so there is a
single spelling per word and only the linking and medd choices remain open,
and the lattice is scored against the templates of the printed meter alone.
The emission and transition probabilities are then learned by EM ( Dempster et al., 1977 ) with
add- λ \lambda smoothing ( λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 ) until the likelihood per line stops
improving. We observed that training everything at once
caused a collapse for the 𝖪 \mathsf{K} emission. With the skip transitions available from the start, skipping a
position is cheaper than emitting 𝖪 \mathsf{K} , so the kept-consonant label never
gathers counts. We therefore train in two stages. The first learns the
emissions with the insert and skip states removed; the second fixes the
emissions of the long, short and free states and learns the transitions, the
meter prior and the insert emissions with the states back in place.

This is the only previous scanner for
Ottoman verse (§ 1 ) that we are aware of. It weighs each syllable of a transcribed

mismatches over the poem, and labels the mismatches medd, linking, zihaf or imâle by its rules. No code

Thus, we first run the restorer for each word to recover the diacritics and use the result as input to their rule-based algorithm.
We also run the algorithm on the plain letters with no restoration, every vowel counted short, so that the
restorer’s share of the result can be read off.

A neural sequence labeler ( Lample et al., 2016 ) trained with the same
supervision as our model, to show what a standard tagger makes of the printed
meter alone. It reads the plain letters of a line character by character,
predicts the poem’s meter, and labels each syllable with its position in that
meter; a separate output head restores the spelling. Since no syllable is
labeled in the training data, it is trained to maximize the total
probability of all position sequences that fit the printed meter, which is
the same objective our model’s EM optimizes. Linking is applied by rule and
flaws are read off the predicted positions against the syllables’ weights. Because a neural model’s result varies with its random
initialization, we train five copies with different seeds and report their spread.

To see which parts of the model account for its
result, we retrain and evaluate it with one part removed at a time. Without

blocks.en:
Table 2 gives the main results on the test split. Every system that restores the spelling
identifies the meter of nearly every poem; ours and Opus 5.5 are above 99.8% per poem, restorer + Kurt & Kara at

poem more than the right one does. The systems separate per line, where ours reaches 98.2% against
84.1% for restorer + Kurt & Kara and 92.0% for the tagger. This shows that
meter identification itself is not a hard task. The real task of this work is scansion.

Our model reads 77.6% of the annotated test lines exactly. The nearest system is Opus 5.5 at
63.6%, a difference of +14.0 points ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 , 95% CI
+9.4 to +18.6). 3 3 3 Exact McNemar test ( McNemar, 1947 ) over the 500 test lines,
on the lines where the two systems disagree, with a paired bootstrap confidence interval over the same lines. The
tagger is compared seed by seed. The
tagger reads 55.0% on average and is behind ours on every seed, and Flash reads 40.0%. Restorer + Kurt & Kara
reads 26.8%, and the same algorithm on the
plain letters only 2.4%, every long vowel having become an open syllable in a long position. Flaw F1
ranks the systems in the same order. These results show that our model, built for the task, is better
than out-of-the-box large language models and the previous rule-based scanner. Being a generative model, it also gives
a probability for every decision it makes, the posterior of a reading under the meter, whereas a language model’s
answer comes with no reliable measure of its own confidence ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) .

blocks.en:
Table 3 contains the ablation results. No single part of the model accounts for its results. Without
the HMM, the fewest-flaw rule over the same lattice of five candidates that the HMM receives reads 44.2 points fewer lines; without the
restorer’s probabilities, 49.2 fewer; without the labels 𝖮 \mathsf{O} and 𝖪 \mathsf{K} , 42.4 fewer.
Each of these leaves the model with less than half of its fully read lines, so the restorer’s probabilities, the scoring under
the meter and the labels for the two flaws that the letters hide are each necessary, and the gain over the
baselines comes from deciding them together. A scanner
for aruz has to weigh the spelling behind the plain letters, the flaws the poet
took and the meter of the poem against one another, since none of them is
certain on its own. The structure matters more than the learned values, since keeping
the starting values in place of EM costs 18.2 points, and the restorer’s generalization to unseen words
matters, since the training lexicon in its place costs 40.0 points. Finally, with the edition’s scholarly transcription in place of the restorer’s
candidates, the model reads 90.6% of lines. Of its 22.4 points of error on plain letters, 13.0 are
therefore in the spelling and 9.4 in linking, medd and the flaw labels, which the model gets wrong even when the
spelling is given. Kurt & Kara reads 34.4% of lines from the same scholarly transcription, so most of the
distance between the two systems is in the scansion rules, not in the spelling. A user who trusts a scholarly transcription can therefore give it to the tool
as it is, with its diacritics kept, and read 90.6% of lines rather
than 77.6%; the web tool offers both inputs.

The robustness benchmark of § 4 rewrites the test poems as the

blocks.en: 8 Related Work
blocks.zh: 8 相关工作

blocks.en:
Automatic scansion in NLP has been developed mainly for European verse, as
sequence labeling of stress, with rule-based scanners ( Navarro-Colorado, 2018 ; de la Rosa et al., 2020 ) , HMMs, CRFs and neural
taggers ( Agirrezabal et al., 2016 ; Agirrezabal et al., 2017 ) , and lately
fine-tuned encoder–decoders ( Ruiz Fabo et al., 2026 ) . For the quantitative meters of
Arabic, Persian and Sanskrit, including aruz, work has concentrated on identifying the meter,
by matching the syllable pattern against the inventory ( Abuata and Al-Omari, 2018 ; Terdalkar and Bhattacharya, 2023 ) or by classifying it from the
characters with a neural model ( Yousef et al., 2019 ; Al-shaibani et al., 2020 ; Alyafeai et al., 2023 ; Mutawa and Alrumaih, 2025 ) with relatively little attention to scansion alignment and noisy copies. For Ottoman Turkish
the only system we found is the rule-based scanner of Kurt and Kara (2012) , which reads
syllable weights off a hand-made scholarly transcription and counts
mismatches. The handbooks ( İpekten, 2010 ; Saraç, 2007 ) , Çetin (1991) and Düzenli and Bulak (2018) describe the flaws qualitatively.

blocks.en:
Restoring what an orthography omits has been studied as diacritic restoration ( Mihalcea and Nastase, 2002 ; Belinkov and Glass, 2015 ; Adalı and Eryiğit, 2014 ) , with the restored
form as the end product. Our restorer is a joint-sequence model of the kind
built for grapheme-to-phoneme conversion ( Bisani and Ney, 2008 ) . Here the
restored form is one of several readings a line admits, and which is right
depends on a meter that is itself unknown, so restoration and scansion are one joint
search, a lattice of readings decoded by an HMM ( Rabiner, 1989 ) with the match, insert and skip structure of a profile HMM ( Krogh et al., 1994 ; Durbin et al., 1998 ) .

作为最终产品。 我们的修复者是那种联合序列模型

blocks.en: 9 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 9 结论

blocks.en:
We addressed the scansion of Ottoman Divan poetry mainly from the plain modern
spelling, with capabilities on scholarly editions as well. We built a corpus of
52,000 lines with scansion annotations for 500 test lines, a robustness
benchmark from the deviation rates measured on web and OCR copies, and a model
that decides spelling, linking and position together, trained from the printed
meter of each poem alone. On held-out poets it reads 77.6% of
lines fully correctly, ahead of the comparable models.
The ablations and error analysis show that joint decoding is critical for this task. Spelling, linking and position are each uncertain on their own
and also reliant on the others. Systems that fix any one of them before
the rest tend to perform worse. The learned flaw rates agree with
the philological account without annotation. We open-source the code and release the scansion tool on the web.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
The scansion annotation was made by an ensemble of large language models under a written guide,
with agreement measured and 200 lines hand-checked. A wider test set that is hand annotated by multiple experts would be helpful in further error analysis with the hopes of producing better and more robust models. The inventory covers fourteen meters; 124 of the 1,731
test poems fall outside it and are not scored, and the model does not report
that a poem fits no meter. The robustness benchmark is generated from measured
deviation rates, not from the real copies, whose transcriptions may be
protected. The benchmark is also released as a pipeline rather than as a full dataset, as the editions of the poems are protected.

Every letter-level edit seen in an aligned word pair is kept with one letter of context
on its left and two on its right, and its rate is the number of times it was made over the number of times its
context occurs in the edition words of the same copies; an edit enters the table when seen at least twice (web
126 edits, OCR 1946). It counts as damage when it changed the word’s
weights in at least half of its occurrences, else as forms. One table thus covers modernization, inserted and
doubled vowels, OCR confusions and typing errors, each at its own rate. Substitutions draw an observed triple
(letter similarity, syllable-count difference, weights kept or changed) and a training-vocabulary word that matches
it; dropped izafets, dropped, added, split and joined words, line numbers, footnote digits and citations (clutter) occur at
their measured rates and in their observed styles; on the web profile a couplet is left out (structure) with probability
10.5%. Each poem draws one intensity from the observed per-document rates
(0.33 to 1.73 times the web profile), since real sources differ in how
much they deviate ( Náplava et al., 2021 ) , and one copy deviates at one rate throughout. Two factors per profile, one on the
forms rates and one on the damage rates (web 2.83 and 1.25, OCR
1.15 and 0.91), bring the generated copy close to the measured word
deviations per word and share of lines whose weights differ; the web forms factor is large because the web survey is
small and only edits seen twice enter the table. Table 7 compares the generated files with the
real copies on these two measures and on three that are not fitted. Every system receives the same word list from
a copy. The text goes through the normalizer, is split on spaces and stripped of punctuation, and tokens without a
vowel are dropped. A line number is therefore invisible to all systems, a footnote digit glued to a word is seen by
the restorer’s lookup and by the tagger, and a citation adds words.
